newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing shuns airbus limelight, Airbus flies high.
newsitem.headline: Boeing shuns airbus limelight, Airbus flies high.

text.p: European aircraft consortium Airbus has used this week's Paris air show to announce potential new business worth some $3.5 billion in contrast with arch-rival Boeing which has kept a low profile.

While past air shows in Britain and France have crackled with the competitive tension between Airbus Industrie and U.S. Boeing Co, there was a sense that this time round, the Seattle-based firm was not looking for a fight.

Industry executives here believe that Boeing is being careful not to attract too much attention in Europe, while the European Commission competition authorities probe its planned $14 billion merger with McDonnell Douglas. A ruling is expected by the end of July.
Airbus's triumphant tone in its Thursday announcement was met with silence from Boeing, whose highly-polished communications machine might normally have had a counterblast prepared.

Yet on close inspection the Airbus announcement embraced firm orders for just four planes worth up to an estimated $290 million, with the rest of the business comprising commitment to buy but not firm orders.

The four-nation consortium also said on Thursday that U.S. Northwest Airlines had signed a memorandum of understanding to order 50 A319 jets with options on up to 100 more. The orders would be worth around $2 billion, based on an average price of $40 million per plane, representing the bulk of Airbus' airshow announcements.

At the last Paris airshow two years ago Boeing flew in its 777 giant twinjet and announced it would make a stretched version of the plane. But so far at this show all boeing has shown off is a niche product, the 737 Boeing business jet.

Industry analysts believe Boeing is concentrating on its merger with McDonnell Douglas which would create a corporation with an annual turnover of $48 billion, dwarfing Airbus which had revenues of $8.8 billion in 1996.
Airbus argues that the merger will create a market dominance aimed at eventually killing it off.
Boeing holds a share of around 60 percent of the world market, while Airbus has some 30 percent with McDonnell Douglas holding the rest.

President of Boeing's Commercial Airplane Group Ron Woodard told reporters earlier this week that McDonnell Douglas sold three planes last year and held a three percent share of the market. "Douglas are in a declining position in the world market," he said.

Woodward also played down the importance of Boeing's exclusive supply deals with U.S. companies, AMR's American Airlines, Delta Air Line and Continental, saying the airlines themselves had asked for the sole-supplier terms.
With the world airline industry climbing strongly out of a deep recession in the early and mid-1990s, Boeing is pushing out aircraft as fast as it can to keep up with demand.

Boeing this year will be building 40 planes a month, more than the previous record 39.5 in 1992, and will aim for 43 in 1998, Woodard said. The previous peak was just before a wave of order cancellations smashed through the industry.
Airbus managing director Jean Pierson earlier said the consortium partners will make modest investments to increase production facilities to handle more output.

Although the investment was small, the fact it was being made at all was significant, an Airbus spokesman said. The partners believed demand would be sustained rather than short-term, or they would have increased overtime working.

Airbus expects to deliver 185 aircraft this year and 220 in 1998. That compares with 126 last year. Pierson said the mix of deliveries would probably be two-thirds narrow-body and one third wide-body aircraft. The wide-bodies carry higher margins.
Airbus believes demand will be durable as airlines which deferred purchases or refitted planes to meet tougher noise limits are coming round to renewing their fleets.
So far this year Airbus has racked up 80 firm orders and 67 commitments, with an undisclosed number of intentions-to-buy, a second Airbus spokesman said.
Boeing has forecast deliveries for 1997 of around 340 planes of all models.
Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz Aerospace, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
